paras: The Round Oak dance killings took place on the night of Monday, December 26, 1881, at a Black dance near Round Oak in Jones County, Georgia, where a young white farmer named Gray was fatally stabbed in a fight and shot dead three Black brothers named Jackson before dying himself. A brief Macon dispatch carried the story to papers from Maine to Texas, which headlined the four deaths at a "negro dance."

Round Oak lay in Jones County, which the Macon dispatch placed forty miles from that city. According to a fuller account printed by the Savannah Morning News on December 31, a "colored dance" was held that Monday night at Dick Richards' place near Round Oak. Two or three young white men attended, among them Jack William Gray and a man identified only as Mr. Green.

In the wire version, Gray "interfered with" the dance and was fatally stabbed by three brothers, Bob, Henry and a third whose name varied from paper to paper. The Savannah account said instead that Gray "became in some way involved in a quarrel" with one of the brothers, and that the quarrel ended in a fight in which he was stabbed. Sinking to the floor, Gray opened fire on the brothers: one fell dead at his feet, a second dropped at the door, and the third got outside and died a few hours later. Gray then crawled out of the house and died on the steps.

Gray was buried the following Tuesday afternoon. The Savannah paper wrote that, as far as it could learn, whisky was "as usual, the cause of the trouble." No report of an inquest, arrest or other legal proceeding appears in the coverage, and none of the accounts quotes anyone who was at the dance.

The first reports came from a single Macon dispatch dated December 28, which ran the next day in the Savannah Morning News, the Chicago Daily Tribune, the Wheeling Register, the National Republican in Washington, the Dallas Daily Herald and the Delaware Daily Gazette, among others. Most headlines simply counted the dead, such as "Four Men Killed in a Row" in Wheeling, "A Terrible Tragedy—Four Dead" in Washington and "Four Deaths at a Dance" in Delaware, while Savannah's read "Terrible Tragedy in Jones County." Two papers went further: the Portland Daily Press headed the item "A Dying Man Kills Three of His Murderers," and the Chicago Tribune's subhead said Gray "Broke Up a Negro Dance" before the brothers stabbed him.

Weeklies kept the item in crime roundups into January 1882. Mississippi's Weekly Clarion ran the wire text on January 4 among lynching and shooting briefs, and the Watertown Republican in Wisconsin placed it among "Tragical Tales," saying Gray fired "into the assemblage." New Jersey's Gloucester County Democrat condensed it on January 5, describing Gray as "a young white planter" who "got into an altercation" with the brothers. The reprints garbled the names, giving Gray as Wm., William, J. W., Jack W. or John W., and the third brother as Alex, Alexander, Alfred, "Aix," "Nix" or Dick.

Accounts differed on how the confrontation began. The wire said Gray interfered with the dance, and the Chicago Tribune that he broke it up, while the Savannah account described a quarrel with one brother and the Gloucester County Democrat an altercation with all three. All of these are white-press versions, and all agree that the brothers stabbed Gray before he fired. The third brother was Alex or Alexander in the Savannah follow-up and most wire copies but Dick in the Watertown digest.

reader.title: Round Oak dance killings
bases: Every report describes a fight at a Black dance in which one white man, Gray, was stabbed and shot three Black brothers dead before dying himself; no mob, band, posse or attack on a community is reported (A1, A12, A18).

The Macon wire report (A1, A3) and the separate, fuller Savannah Morning News account apparently drawn from the Macon Telegraph (A12) agree on the core event: Gray stabbed at a dance, three Jackson brothers shot dead, Gray dead on the steps; both trace to Macon sources.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Macon dispatch under neutral death-count headlines: 'Four Men Killed in a Row', 'A Terrible Tragedy—Four Dead', 'Four Deaths at a Dance'.
The Portland Daily Press headed it 'A Dying Man Kills Three of His Murderers', casting the brothers as murderers, while the Chicago Tribune's subhead said Gray 'Broke Up a Negro Dance'.
The Savannah Morning News called it a 'Terrible Tragedy' and, in its follow-up, said whisky was 'as usual, the cause of the trouble'.
